pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: You have manifests for one service and three environments that differ by a few numbers. What goes wrong if you just copy the directory three times, and what do Helm and Kustomize each do about it?
expected_points: copies drift: a fix lands in one copy and not the others, and nothing warns you — three directories of legal YAML that no longer agree about what the service is
both make one description authoritative and the differences explicit
Helm generates the manifests from templates filled in by values
Kustomize keeps plain manifests as a base and each environment is a small patch listing only what differs

questions.prompt: Walk me through your chart. What is in Chart.yaml, what is values.yaml for, and what is _helpers.tpl doing?
expected_points: Chart.yaml: apiVersion v2 (Helm 3), name, description, and two different versions — version is the chart's own, appVersion is the software it installs
values.yaml holds the defaults and is the chart's public API: every key is a promise an installer can set and the next version has to keep
put in it only what an installer must be able to change; the rest stays literal in the templates
templates render with .Values, .Chart and .Release; _helpers.tpl defines named templates included everywhere, so the name and the selector labels cannot disagree between two files
the Deployment's spec.selector is immutable, so a name that disagrees is not always fixable in place

questions.prompt: Describe your kustomize base and overlays. What is allowed to live in an overlay, and what is not?
expected_points: a directory is a kustomization because it contains kustomization.yaml; the base holds everything true everywhere and knows nothing about environments
each overlay lists the base directory under resources, plus its differences: namespace, replicas, patch files
a patch is a partial manifest: identity (apiVersion, kind, metadata.name, the container's name) plus only the fields that differ
the merge is strategic — maps merge key by key and lists of objects merge by name — so patching resources leaves the probes and env alone
an overlay may change how much of something an environment gets, never whether the service works: probes, drain settings and security context stay in the base

questions.prompt: Someone changes only a log level. How does that reach the running pods in Kustomize, and how in Helm? What breaks if you turn either mechanism off?
expected_points: env vars from envFrom are snapshotted when the container is created, so editing a ConfigMap alone leaves running pods on the old values

Kustomize: configMapGenerator appends a hash of the content to the name and rewrites every reference, so a changed literal means a new name, a new pod template and a rollout — and the old ConfigMap survives, so rolling back the manifests rolls back the config
Helm: no generator, so the chart hashes the rendered ConfigMap into a checksum/config pod-template annotation, which changes the pod template and rolls the Deployment
both work by changing the pod template — that is the only thing that causes a rollout
disableNameSuffixHash: true, or a dropped annotation, means the upgrade reports success, the ConfigMap holds the new value, and the pods keep serving the old one

questions.prompt: Internal service across dev/staging/prod, versus software other organisations install into clusters you'll never see. Which tool for each, and what does each choice cost you?
expected_points: Helm for software you distribute: a chart is a versioned artifact fetched by name and version, values.yaml is a documented API with defaults, and install/upgrade/rollback/uninstall are one tool's job
Kustomize for your own environments: a few values do not need a templating language, plain YAML keeps working in editors and reviews, and what you read is what applies
Helm's cost is templating pain forever — untypechecked text templating over whitespace-significant YAML
Kustomize's cost is the release lifecycle: no artifact and no stored revisions, so rollback is git revert plus apply, which is only as good as git being the record of what is deployed
the deciding question is who changes this and how they get it, not which is better

questions.prompt: How do you see what a one-line change actually produces before it touches a cluster — in each system — and how do you see it as a diff against what is running? Then tell me what a rollback is in each.
expected_points: helm template <release> ./chart renders to stdout and contacts nothing; kubectl kustomize (or kustomize build) does the same for an overlay
against the live state: helm upgrade --dry-run or the helm-diff plugin, and kubectl diff -k for the overlay
review the rendered manifests, not the templates — a one-line values change can move a lot of YAML, and the render is the only honest description of what will happen
Helm rollback is specific: every revision is stored in the cluster (a Secret in the release namespace), so helm rollback <release> <n> re-applies revision n with no files on your side
Kustomize has no release history: rollback means checking out the previous commit and applying again

questions.prompt: Why is templated YAML a category of bug on its own, and what is the discipline that keeps it manageable?
expected_points: Go templates produce text, not YAML, and YAML is whitespace-significant — a whitespace-chomping {{- that eats one newline too many splices two keys onto one line
the error names a line in the rendered output you cannot see, not a line in your template
nothing type-checks values: a misspelled path renders empty and ships a key with no value; editors' YAML support is useless inside a template
the discipline is to render every time — helm template is the debugger — and read the manifests rather than the templates

questions.prompt: Can you use both together? When is that a good idea and when is it a smell?
expected_points: helm template output is just manifests, so a chart can become the base of a kustomization; Helm can also call kustomize as a post-renderer
legitimate when somebody else's chart needs a change their values.yaml does not expose
a smell on a chart you control — the fix there is to expose the value, because you own the API
the cost is that you now run two tools and the release lifecycle only knows about one of them
